articles.title: Meta Launches Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full: Benchmarks, Pricing and How to Use It
articles.content: Meta has released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, its most capable models so far. Muse Wonder is a frontier model from Meta built for personal and professional AI agents. Both models target long-running agent work: coding, legal and finance tasks, and computer use. Muse Wonder is live now on the Meta Model API and Muse Code. Muse Wonder Full is limited to paid Muse Code plans. TL;DR Size: 1M-token context, input of text, image, video and audio, output of text. Runs on: Meta’s cloud only, via the API or Muse Code CLI (macOS, Linux, Windows). Performance: Muse Wonder Full leads 6 of 14 rows in Meta’s benchmark table. It trails Claude Opus 5.5 on several. Best: Muse Wonder scores 85.6 on MemoryBench, the top result among all 5 models listed. Worst: Muse Wonder scores 50.0 on ProgramBench, against 70.5 for Claude Opus 5.5. What is Muse Wonder? Muse Wonder follows Muse Spark on Meta’s scaling ladder. Meta team states that it was trained at its Prometheus data center, with gains across pretraining and reinforcement learning. Meta credits a larger base model for better results on unfamiliar tasks. Two named behaviors define the release: Active Memory: carries user context across conversations and pulls back the details a task needs. Active Focus: keeps working on hard tasks, tries alternatives, and checks in before important actions. For developers, Muse Wonder plans long tasks and delegates to sub-agents. It also operates browsers, desktop and mobile apps. How does Muse Wonder perform on benchmarks? All scores below come from Meta’s published table at max reasoning effort. Several rows use third-party sources such as Artificial Analysis, Vals AI and Datacurve. BenchmarkMuse Wonder FullMuse WonderClaude Fable 5.1GPT-6 AstraClaude Opus 5.5Personal Superintelligence Index (internal)59.154.349.954.555.2Harvey LAB-AA13.110.06.48.64.2Vals Finance Agent V259.156.658.953.558.6AutomationBench-AA45.439.132.141.641.2OSWorld V2.1 (partial)78.472.680.775.881.8MemoryBench (internal)85.585.679.081.481.5Terminal-Bench 4.0-AA57.152.052.059.159.6DeepSWE 1.179.078.867.474.174.2SWE-Marathon57.5 (xhigh)53.145.642.546.3ProgramBench59.050.055.552.570.5AA Intelligence Index v4.35652535358 Note: PSI, MemoryBench and FocusBench are internal Meta evaluations. The model card says competitor runs are best-effort and may not be tuned. SWE-Marathon results for rivals used Codex and Claude Code, so it is not a common-harness comparison. && Muse Wonder vs Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra FeatureMuse WonderMuse Wonder FullClaude Opus 5.5Claude Fable 5.1GPT-6 AstraDeveloperMetaMetaAnthropicAnthropicOpenAIParametersNot disclosedNot disclosedNot disclosedNot disclosedNot disclosedContext1M1M1M1M1.05MInput modalitiesText, image, video, audioText, image, video, audioText, imageText, imageText, imageOpen weightsNoNoNoNoNoAPI price (in / out per 1M)$4 / $20Subscription only$4 / $20$10 / $50$10 / $50AccessModel API, Muse CodeMuse Code Power ($50) or Maximum ($200)Claude APIClaude APIOpenAI APIDeepSWE 1.178.879.074.267.474.1 How to use Muse Wonder: step-by-step for new users Step 1: Open dev.meta.ai. Click Start building to sign in. The Muse Code install command sits on the same page. Step 2: Pick your model. Muse Wonder costs $4 input, $0.20 cached and $20 output per million tokens. Muse Wonder Full needs a Muse Code plan: Power at $50 or Maximum at $200 per month. Step 3: Sign in with your Meta account. Confirm your name, accept the Model API terms, and click Get started. Step 4. Add billing, then create an API key. New accounts see a “No payment method” banner, and Create API key stays disabled. Add a card under Billing, then open API keys and select Create API key. Export it as MODEL_API_KEY, per the quickstart. Step 5. Test it in the Playground. Open Chat, pick muse-wonder-1.0, and set temperature, max tokens and reasoning effort. Step 6. Copy working code. Click Get code for a curl or Python snippet. It calls the Responses endpoint at https://api.meta.ai/v1/responses. The API is OpenAI-compatible, so the OpenAI SDK works with a new base URL: Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browserimport os from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.meta.ai/v1", api_key=os.environ["MODEL_API_KEY"]) resp = client.responses.create(model="muse-wonder-1.0", input="List 3 risks in this lease clause: ...") print(resp.output_text) Step 7: Or use Muse Code in your terminal. On Mac, install with curl -fsSL https://dev.meta.ai/install.sh | bash. On Windows, use irm https://dev.meta.ai/install.ps1 | iex. Run muse in your project folder, trust the workspace, and sign in. The default model is muse-spark-1.2. Switch with /models, or launch with muse --model muse-wonder-1.0. Key Takeaways Muse Wonder ships at $4/$20 per million tokens with 1M context. Muse Wonder Full leads DeepSWE (79.0) and SWE-Marathon (57.5). Claude Opus 5.5 still leads ProgramBench, OSWorld and Terminal-Bench. Wonder Full is Muse Code only, from $50 per month. No parameters, open weights or full safety report yet. Check out the research blog, model card and developer docs. All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter. Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. articles.summary: Meta가 코딩·법률·금융·컴퓨터 사용 등 장시간 에이전트 작업을 겨냥한 Muse Wonder와 Muse Wonder Full을 출시했다는 보도다. 두 모델은 100만 토큰 문맥과 텍스트·이미지·영상·음성 입력을 지원하며, 대화 간 사용자 맥락을 활용하는 Active Memory와 어려운 작업을 지속적으로 수행하는 Active Focus를 내세운다. 기사에 인용된 Meta 평가표에서 Full은 14개 항목 중 6개에서 선두였지만, 여러 항목에서는 Claude Opus 5.5에 뒤져 전반적인 우위로 해석하기는 어렵다. Muse Wonder는 Meta Model API와 Muse Code에서 제공되며, Full은 유료 Muse Code 요금제로 접근이 제한된다.

articles.title: Z.ai GLM-Legal Beats Claude Fable 5 and Kimi K3 on Harvey LAB
articles.content: Z.ai just released GLM-Legal. GLM-Legal is a legal AI model from Z.ai, built on GLM-5.3-Flash and trained for agentic legal work. It targets contract review, evidence analysis and compliance research. The key result is a 19.2% all-pass rate on Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB). That is nearly 3x its base model’s 6.7%. For developers, the catch is access: the API is application-only for now. TL;DR Size: Built on GLM-5.3-Flash, a 320B-total, 18B-active MoE with a 1M-token context and 128K max output. Z.ai lists no separate GLM-Legal parameter count. Runs on: Z.ai’s hosted API only, by application. No public weights. The base model self-hosts on multi-GPU servers via vLLM or SGLang, with FP8 weights. Performance: Top-10 on Harvey LAB at a fraction of frontier cost. Within 2.3 points of the LegalBench leader. Best: 19.17% Harvey LAB task pass rate, #7 of 79 on Vals AI, at $0.15 per test. Worst: 41.83% on Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench, below its own base model (45.19%). Bottom line: Best: frontier-class legal agent scores at about 1/128 the cost of Claude Fable 5. Worst: gated beta with no price, no weights and slow runs (1h12m per task). What is GLM-Legal? GLM-Legal is a domain-specialized version of GLM-5.3-Flash for law firms, in-house counsel and compliance teams. The base is Z.ai’s first natively multimodal GLM-5 model. It has 320B total parameters with 18B active. It mixes sparse and linear attention to cut long-context serving cost. It reads text, images, video and files, and outputs text. How was GLM-Legal trained? Training ran in 2 stages: Mid-training on expanded legal corpora, to strengthen reasoning from facts to rules to conclusions. Post-training with reinforcement learning across tens of thousands of legal task environments. The Z.ai team also describes the agent harness co-evolving with the model during post-training. Edge cases in training exposed harness bottlenecks. Harness fixes then exposed the model to more realistic constraints. How does GLM-Legal score on Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark? Harvey LAB is an open-source benchmark of 1,250 tasks across 24 practice areas. Over 75,000 expert-written rubric criteria grade the work. A task passes only if every criterion passes. Harvey calls this all-pass grading. Vals AI runs the held-out set with 2 LLM judges and internet disabled. Agents get file tools plus docx, pptx and xlsx skills. On that leaderboard, GLM-Legal scores 19.17% and ranks #7 of 79. Its base, GLM-5.3-Flash, scores 6.67%. The 12.5-point lift is the core claim, and an independent evaluator reproduced it. Z.ai’s launch chart shows GLM-Legal ahead of Kimi K3 (12.92%), Claude Fable 5 (11.25%) and GPT-6 Astra (5.42%). Those figures match Vals AI. The chart omits 6 models ranked higher, led by Muse Spark 1.2 at 25.42%. GLM-Legal also passes 92.5% of individual criteria. Top models sit near 90% to 95% on that measure. Does GLM-Legal match frontier models on LegalBench? Roughly. Z.ai claims parity on LegalBench and the Chinese-focused PLawBench without publishing numbers. Vals AI scores GLM-Legal at 86.23% on LegalBench. Claude Fable 5 leads at 88.56%. Kimi K3 scores 86.21%. &&& How does GLM-Legal compare with Kimi K3, Claude Fable 5 and GPT-6 Astra? Vals ran both GLM models at $0.075 / $0.25 per 1M tokens. How can developers access GLM-Legal? Law firms, legal-tech companies and in-house teams can apply for API access. Z.ai has published no price. No GLM-Legal repository exists on Hugging Face as of October 13, 2026. Z.ai says GLM-Legal will come to AutoClaw, its desktop agent app, but gave no date. The base model is available today at $0.15 / $0.50 per 1M tokens. Teams can prototype pipelines on it, then swap the model ID later. Key Takeaways GLM-Legal scores 19.17% on Harvey LAB, up from 6.67% for its base. It ranks #7 of 79 on Vals AI, behind 6 Meta and Google models. It costs $0.15 per Harvey LAB test, versus $19.23 for Claude Fable 5. Legal Research Bench dropped 3.36 points versus GLM-5.3-Flash. Access is application-only, with no published price or weights. Check out the Z.ai tech blog, the Vals AI Harvey LAB leaderboard and the GLM-5.3-Flash model card. Apply for API access here.. All credit goes to the researcher of this project. articles.title: Google Play now lets anyone build private, vibe-coded apps that run on Android
articles.content: Google is making it easier to build and use personal Android apps created with AI, without having to make them available to everyone on the Play Store.
articles.summary: Google이 AI로 만든 개인용 Android 앱을 Play Store에 일반 공개하지 않고도 제작·사용하기 쉽게 하는 기능을 선보였다. AI를 활용한 앱 개발을 공개 배포와 분리해 개인 목적의 소프트웨어 활용 경로를 넓힌다는 점이 핵심이다. 개인 맞춤형 앱의 제작과 사용 장벽을 낮출 수 있지만, 제공된 자료에는 지원 도구와 배포 절차, 보안 검증 방식이 설명돼 있지 않다.

articles.title: Amex introduces a framework to prevent AI agents from making unauthorized purchases
articles.content: American Express is introducing a new framework designed to ensure AI agents only make purchases their users have authorized, potentially preventing costly mistakes and disputes as AI-powered shopping grows.
articles.summary: American Express가 AI 에이전트가 사용자에게 승인받은 구매만 수행하도록 하는 프레임워크를 도입한다. 에이전트의 구매 실행을 사용자 승인 범위에 연결해 잘못된 결제와 분쟁을 줄이는 것이 목적이다. AI 쇼핑의 실제 결제 단계에 통제 장치를 마련한다는 의미가 있지만, 제공된 자료에는 승인 검증 기술이나 적용 대상의 세부사항이 없다.

articles.title: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world
articles.content: University of Michigan spinout Laplace Intelligence uses AI agents and interactive simulation to stress-test robots and self-driving vehicles before deployment. The profitable startup is competing in Startup Battlefield at TechCrunch Disrupt, October 13-15 in San Francisco.
articles.summary: 미시간대학교에서 분사한 Laplace Intelligence가 AI 에이전트와 상호작용형 시뮬레이션을 활용해 로봇과 자율주행 차량을 배포 전에 스트레스 테스트한다. 실제 환경에 투입하기 전 시스템의 취약한 행동을 점검하는 레드팀 접근이 핵심이다. 물리적 시스템의 사전 안전성 검증에 활용될 수 있지만, 제공된 자료에는 탐지 성능이나 실제 사고 감소 효과를 입증하는 수치가 없다.

articles.title: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
articles.content: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here. Late last month, Anthropic released a report arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk. The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify. Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs.  These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models. “I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information. Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely. There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly. But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization. Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth. What are the benefits of open models? Let’s start with the basics. A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API. An open model, on the other hand, can be directly downloaded: The details about its internal structure, encoded in a long series of numbers known as the model weights, are publicly available. Such models are sometimes called “open-weight models,” to distinguish them from models for which even more information, such as details about the training procedure, is available.  Right now, closed models are more capable than open models—as of publication, the top eight models on the Artificial Analysis LLM leaderboard are all closed, though open models are only a handful of months behind in development. But there are several reasons why someone might opt to use an open model rather than a closed one. Because open models are downloadable, people can run them on their own computers or hard drives. They can even retrain them to behave differently, if they have the expertise and resources to do so. If you’re an academic researcher working to understand and improve AI systems, you almost certainly need to work with open models in your research. When working with closed models, researchers can’t do much more than send prompts and observe the responses. But researchers can observe the inner workings of open models, as well as the “chain of thought” that the models use to think through a problem before answering. They can also combine multiple open models to build new systems, compress them to make them more efficient, and fine-tune them for new applications. Businesses, too, have reasons to prefer open models. Even if you depend on an external provider to run them for you, open models still typically cost less than closed models, according to a recent report from Mozilla. And if businesses want to use AI to process sensitive data or proprietary information, running a local model on their own hardware may be the best way to keep their operations secure. But perhaps the most important quality of open models is that they challenge the tight control the frontier labs have over how most of us use AI. “The clearest, biggest argument [for open models] is around preventing mass concentration of power—it is about making sure that this foundational technology is a public good,” says Elizabeth Seger, senior policy advisor at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. “I think we’re at this juncture where the question of who controls the infrastructure that allows AI to operate is as big of a question as who gets to control information on the internet.” Seger sees the future of AI playing out in different ways, depending on the role that open models have. In one possible future, frontier AI systems are controlled entirely by select people, companies, or governments, and as those systems grow more powerful, those groups have increasing control over what our world looks like. The world’s most sophisticated hacking models, for example, are currently all made in the United States, so it’s entirely up to US companies and the US government whether other countries can use them to shore up their own cyber defenses. If those companies remain in the lead, we could in principle wind up in a world in which the United States is capable of hacking any other country, but no one is capable of hacking it. Frontier open models could change that balance. “If every individual had a loyal-to-them AI system that was safe [and secure], I think that would be a much less concerning world than one in which they have to just rely on a government that says, ‘Yeah, we’ve got a super intelligent AI system, it’s got this plan, it’s inscrutable to all of you, just trust us,’” says Hamish Hobbs, director of AI policy at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience. But open models are not a geopolitical panacea. Paul Azunre, who cofounded Ghana NLP, an organization that builds open-source AI tools for low-resource Ghanaian languages, notes that open models can also function as a way for companies to benefit from the labor and expertise of less-privileged nations and consolidate more power in their own hands. He identifies a pattern in which AI companies release models openly, observe how the community uses and modifies them, and then integrate those same improvements into their own products—without any credit or compensation for the people who originated those innovations. Mark Zuckerberg himself has said that the ability to integrate community improvements into Meta’s stack is a key benefit of releasing open models. “I think the ideal of open source is a very noble one, and there’s a lot of value that it brings,” Azunre says. “But the way it’s actually implemented in practice, it tends to be a very extractive approach.” Are open models riskier than closed ones? The past few months have made it clear that safety remains a gnarly problem for closed models. There’s the autonomous hack that OpenAI agents executed against Hugging Face in July, but human misuse is a real threat too: According to a recent risk report from Anthropic, several extensive hacking operations have been undertaken with the assistance of Claude. So closed models are risky enough—and open models would likely be much easier to exploit. Before Anthropic passes a user’s query to one of its closed models, it uses automated systems to detect whether that query relates to hacking, biological weapons, or other risks. When it detects that users have outsmarted those filters, it can shut down their accounts. But when someone downloads a model and runs it on their own hardware, there’s no filter checking whether their prompts are safe, and there’s no way to revoke their access to the model. There are other important lines of defense. AI companies train their models to refuse harmful requests—so even if a bad prompt gets through Claude’s filters, there’s a good chance that the model will still say no. In principle, this same defense could work for open models, because it’s intrinsic to the model itself. Unfortunately, researchers have shown that it’s surprisingly easy to retrain a “safe” open model to agree to engage in the behaviors it was previously trained to avoid. Because of these facts, some people have argued that open models are simply too dangerous to release. An open model capable enough to walk someone through synthesizing a virulent new pathogen, for example, could prove catastrophic in the wrong hands.  But it would be a vast oversimplification to deem open models dangerous and closed models safe. The defenses that AI companies build around their closed models are far from perfect, and people misuse those models all the time, as the Anthropic risk report makes clear. Even though open models have even fewer defenses against misuse, bad actors might still opt to use closed models because they are more accessible than open models with similar capabilities, which require lots of expensive computer chips to run locally (and even more chips if you want to retrain them). In fact, some experts who spoke with MIT Technology Review argued, by analogy to open-source software, that open models have safety advantages over closed models. Open-source tools, such as the Linux operating system, are often seen as safer than their closed-source counterparts because their vulnerabilities have been probed and patched by a vast community of online contributors. Similarly, communities of researchers can more easily test open models for security flaws, though fixing those flaws is trickier than rewriting a line of code. Open models can also be deployed more broadly than closed models for cyber defense. Any tool that can be used for hacking can also be used to prevent it: Defenders hack their own software to uncover flaws in need of patching. Anthropic has shown
articles.summary: MIT Technology Review가 공개 AI 모델의 접근성·활용 이점과 악용 위험 사이의 논쟁을 다뤘다. 기사는 Anthropic이 다운로드와 수정이 가능한 Z.ai의 GLM-5.3을 주요 사이버공격 위험으로 지목했다고 전하면서, 공개 모델 지지와 신중론 양쪽에 상업적 이해관계도 작용한다고 설명한다. 핵심 쟁점은 강력한 AI의 활용 기회를 넓히면서 악용을 어떻게 통제할지이며, 선택지가 전면 금지와 무제한 공개의 양극단에만 있지는 않다는 점이다. 제공된 자료만으로 특정 모델의 실제 위험 수준이나 최적의 규제 방식을 확정할 수는 없다.

articles.title: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
articles.content: When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says. The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going ­belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs. SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales. And it’s got company. Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business. Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools. Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.”  Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets. Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs. Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls. Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined. Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear. No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives. Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code. That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening. This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data, including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records. The price tag: $10 million. And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups. Legally, this all could get iffy. Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too. But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans. He describes a “Wild West of AI training” that is only starting to give way to proper licensing agreements and vetted use. There’s also the question of who profits from these windfalls. The proceeds typically flow to senior creditors and investors—not employees. To Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University and author of The Quantified Worker, this represents a form of “captured capital.” Legal precedent allows for monitoring to help workers do their jobs, but once a firm is out of business, that justification vanishes. “Employers should have express consent before selling workers’ data,” says Ajunwa, but she adds that there’s no federal law banning such sales. While many see this new market as a chance for failing businesses to recover some value, these wind-down sales also have limitations. Founders have little to no visibility into who is buying the data and what they plan to do with it. Plus, there’s little assurance they’re getting a fair offer. Data prices will likely stabilize in the coming year, though, unless an AI bubble pops first. Either way, tech’s new undertakers will be there to appraise what’s left.  Matthew King is a technology and environmental journalist based in Baltimore.
articles.summary: AI 연구소와 학습 환경 공급업체들이 폐업하는 스타트업의 코드·이메일·채팅·문서 등 업무 데이터를 구매하고 있다고 MIT Technology Review가 보도했다. 중개업체 SimpleClosure의 Asset Hub는 150건 이상의 거래를 처리했으며, 회사는 2026년 말까지 스타트업에 돌아가는 금액이 1,000만 달러를 넘을 것으로 예상한다. 실제 조직의 업무 흔적이 모델 학습과 모의 업무 환경 구축을 위한 자산으로 전환되고 있다는 점이 중요하다. 다만 제공된 자료에는 데이터별 이용 동의, 권리 처리 및 비식별화 절차가 구체적으로 제시되지 않았다.

articles.title: 딥엘, 중앙대 전문 통번역 교육에 도입…언어·문화 전문성에 AI 활용 역량 더한 통번역 인재 양성
articles.content:
글로벌 언어 인공지능(AI) 기업 딥엘(DeepL)의 번역 기술이 중앙대학교 전문 통번역 교육 과정에 도입됐다. 대학 교육 현장에서 실제 번역 업계가 활용하는 AI 기반 워크플로를 경험할 수 있도록 교육 범위를 확장한 것으로, 언어 전문성과 AI 활용 능력을 겸비한 통번역 인재 양성이 목표다.

딥엘은 14일, 중앙대 국제대학원 전문통번역학과(Advanced Interpretation & Translation Program, AITP) 교육 과정에 ‘딥엘 프로(DeepL Pro)’가 도입됐다고 밝혔다. 중앙대는 국내 대학 가운데 교육 목적으로 딥엘 프로를 도입한 첫 사례라고 회사 측은 설명했다.

중앙대는 올해 3월부터 딥엘을 교육 과정에 활용하고 있다. 기존의 컴퓨터 보조 번역(CAT) 도구 중심 교육에 AI 기반 번역 기술을 추가해 학생들이 실제 산업 현장에서 사용되는 도구와 작업 방식을 익힐 수 있도록 했다.

CAT 도구 중심에서 AI 기반 번역 워크플로로 확대

전문 번역 교육에서 컴퓨터 보조 번역 도구는 번역 메모리와 용어 관리 등 반복적인 작업을 지원하는 핵심 기술로 활용돼 왔다. 중앙대학교는 여기에 AI 기반 언어 처리 기술을 접목해 학생들이 변화하는 번역 업무 환경에 대응할 수 있도록 교육 범위를 넓혔다.

학생들은 딥엘 프로를 활용해 하나의 플랫폼에서 다양한 번역 워크플로를 경험하고, 기존에 쌓아 온 언어 지식과 번역 역량을 AI 기술과 결합하는 방법을 학습한다. 교수진도 언어 AI의 최신 기능과 기술 발전을 수업에 반영할 수 있다.

이준호 중앙대 국제대학원 전문통번역학과 한영번역 전공 교수는 학생들이 졸업 전에 실제 번역 업계에서 사용되는 기술을 경험하도록 하는 것이 도입의 목적이라고 설명했다.

이 교수는 "딥엘을 통해 다양한 번역 작업을 통합된 플랫폼에서 경험할 수 있고, 서비스에 새로운 기능이 추가될 때마다 최신 기술 동향을 교육 과정에 반영할 수 있다" 며, "학생들이 언어 전문성을 바탕으로 AI를 효과적으로 활용하는 방법을 이해하는 데도 도움이 될 것"이라고 말했다.

현업에서 활용되는 언어 AI를 교육 현장에 적용

중앙대가 이번 딥엘을 선택한 배경에는 졸업 이후 실무에서 접할 가능성이 높은 기술을 미리 익히도록 하려는 목적과 번역 업계에서의 활용도가 있다. 딥엘은 유럽 언어 산업 설문조사(European Language Industry Survey, ELIS)를 근거로 자사 서비스가 유럽에서 가장 널리 사용되는 기계번역 도구라고 밝혔다.

중앙대 전문통번역학과는 국내 주요 석사과정 통번역 교육기관 중 하나로, 딥엘 도입 이전에도 대형언어모델(LLM) 기반 컴퓨터 보조 번역 기술을 교육에 활용해 왔다. 이번 도입은 기존의 AI 관련 교육 경험을 실제 언어 AI 서비스 활용으로 확장했다는 점에서 의미가 있다.

야렉 쿠틸로브스키(Jarek Kutylowski) 딥엘 창업자 겸 최고경영자(CEO)는 AI가 전문 번역가를 비롯해 다양한 언어 환경에서 일하는 사람들의 업무 방식을 바꾸면서 관련 산업도 빠르게 변화하고 있다고 밝혔다.

그는 "차세대 인재들이 발전하는 기술을 직접 활용할 기회를 갖는 것이 중요하다며, 중앙대학교와의 협력을 통해 학생들이 언어 AI의 실무 경험을 쌓고 기술이 산업에 미치는 영향을 이해할 수 있을 것으로 기대한다"며, "AI를 활용하더라도 학생 스스로의 판단력과 언어 전문성을 유지하고 이를 보완하는 방식으로 기술을 사용하는 법을 배우게 될 것"이라고 말했다.

AI 활용 능력, 통번역 전문가의 새로운 실무 역량으로

이번 도입은 통번역 교육이 언어와 문화에 대한 전문성을 넘어 AI 기술을 업무에 적용하는 능력까지 포괄하는 방향으로 확대되고 있음을 보여준다.

AI 번역 기술이 전문 업무에 활용되면서 통번역 전문가에게는 번역 결과를 검토하고 맥락과 뉘앙스를 판단하는 능력뿐 아니라, 작업 목적에 맞는 AI 도구를 선택하고 결과물을 효과적으로 활용하는 역량도 중요해지고 있다.

중앙대의 딥엘 프로 도입은 이러한 변화에 대응해 학생들이 교육 단계부터 현업의 AI 기반 번역 환경을 경험하도록 한 사례다. 향후 전문 통번역 교육에서 AI 도구 활용과 인간 전문가의 언어적 판단력을 어떻게 결합할지가 주요 과제로 부상할 전망이다.
articles.summary: 중앙대학교 국제대학원 전문통번역학과가 올해 3월부터 DeepL Pro를 교육 과정에 활용하고 있으며, DeepL은 국내 대학의 교육 목적 도입으로는 첫 사례라고 설명했다. 기존 컴퓨터 보조 번역 도구 중심 교육에 AI 기반 번역 워크플로를 추가해 학생들이 현업 도구와 작업 방식을 경험하도록 한다. 기술 자체의 신규 성능 발표보다는 언어·문화 전문성과 AI 활용 역량을 결합하는 국내 교육 적용 사례라는 의미가 크다. 교육은 AI를 사용하더라도 학생의 판단력과 언어 전문성을 유지하고 보완하는 방향을 지향한다.

articles.title: Industrial Next wants factory robots to switch tasks in minutes, not weeks
articles.content: Industrial Next helps manufacturers automate complex, delicate tasks that have traditionally required human labor.
articles.summary: Industrial Next가 제조 현장에서 사람이 맡아온 복잡하고 섬세한 작업의 자동화를 추진한다. 기사는 공장 로봇의 작업 전환 시간을 수주가 아닌 수분 수준으로 줄이는 것을 회사의 목표로 제시한다. 실현될 경우 여러 작업을 처리해야 하는 제조 현장의 자동화 유연성을 높일 수 있지만, 제공된 자료에는 이를 달성하는 기술 구조나 검증된 전환 시간 수치가 없다.

The binding ignores unknown keys without a warning, so the keys are checked against the TypedDicts in rebalancer.specs: the arm's own keys and the nested limit, affinities and conflict lists used in this notebook.""" check_keys(arm[0].upper() + arm[1:], fields, arm) return {arm: fields} MOVES = {"single": {"singleMoveTypeSpec": {}}, "swap": {"swapMoveTypeSpec": {}}, "triple": {"tripleLoopMoveTypeSpec": {}}, "kl": {"klSearchMoveTypeSpec": {}}} def local_search(seconds=2, seed=0, moves=("single", "swap"), **extra): return spec("localSearchSolverSpec", moveTypeList=[MOVES[m] for m in moves], solveTime=int(seconds), randomSeed=seed, **extra) def highs(seconds=5): # solverPackage 2 is HiGHS, the only MIP solver compiled into the pip wheel. suppressLogs removes a banner that the # optimal path otherwise prints to stdout. return spec("optimalSolverSpec", solverPackage=PACKAGE["HIGHS"], solveTime=int(seconds), suppressLogs=True) def new_problem(assignment, objects="task", containers="host"): p = ProblemSolver(service_name="rebalancer_tutorial", service_scope="marktechpost") p.set_log_level("ERROR") # silences ~50 log lines per solve; never "OFF", which exits the process p.set_object_name(objects).set_container_name(containers) # names first, then the assignment, then dimensions p.set_assignment(assignment) # every container must be listed, empty ones too return p def solve(p): t = time.perf_counter() sol = p.solve() dt = time.perf_counter() - t SOLVE_SECONDS[CURRENT[0]] += dt return sol, dt # Independent checks: everything below reads only the returned assignment, never the solver's own verdict. def where(container_to_objects): return {o: c for c, objs in container_to_objects.items() for o in objs} def by_container(object_to_container, containers): out = {c: [] for c in containers} for o, c in sorted(object_to_container.items()): out[c].append(o) return out def load(object_to_container, values): out = collections.Counter() for o, c in object_to_container.items(): out[c] += values.get(o, 0.0) return out def excess(object_to_container, values, caps): L = load(object_to_container, values) return {c: max(0.0, L[c] - caps[c]) for c in caps} def moved(before, after): return sum(before[o] != after[o] for o in before) def ends(sol): return "/".join(END.get(r["endReason"], str(r["endReason"])) for r in sol["solverSummaries"]) def goals(sol): return [round(g["value"], 6) for g in sol["finalGlobalObjective"]["goals"]] def clean(e, n=90, typed=True): msg = re.sub(r"[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}", "<id>", str(e)).strip()[:n] return f"{type(e).__name__}: {msg}" if typed else msg def cpu_name(): if os.path.exists("/proc/cpuinfo"): for line in open("/proc/cpuinfo"): if line.startswith("model name"): return line.split(":", 1)[1].strip() if sys.platform == "darwin": r = subprocess.run(["sysctl", "-n", "machdep.cpu.brand_string"], capture_output=True, text=True) if r.stdout.strip(): return r.stdout.strip() return platform.processor() or platform.machine() def ram_gb(): if os.path.exists("/proc/meminfo"): kb = next(int(l.split()[1]) for l in open("/proc/meminfo") if l.startswith("MemTotal")) return kb / 1024 ** 2 r = subprocess.run(["sysctl", "-n", "hw.memsize"], capture_output=True, text=True) return int(r.stdout) / 1024 ** 3 if r.stdout.strip() else float("nan") VERSION = md.version("rebalancer") HW = f"{cpu_name()}, {os.cpu_count()} logical CPUs, {ram_gb():.0f} GB RAM" print(f"rebalancer {VERSION} python {platform.python_version()} {platform.system()} {platform.machine()}") print(f"hardware: {HW}") assert VERSION == "1.0.4", "this notebook is written against rebalancer 1.0.4; restart the runtime after installing" def two_tasks(solver_spec, policy=None): # Two 10 GB tasks on host0, two hosts of 15 GB: the start breaks capacity and one task has to move. p = new_problem({"host0": ["t0", "t1"], "host1": []}) p.add_object_dimension("memory", {"t0": 10.0, "t1": 10.0}) p.add_container_dimension("memory", {}, default_value=15.0) kw = {} if policy is None else {"policy": policy} p.add_constraint(spec("capacitySpec", name="memory_capacity", scope="host", dimension="memory"), **kw) p.add_solver(solver_spec) return p GATE = {} for label, make in [("local search", lambda: two_tasks(local_search(2))), ("HiGHS (solverPackage=2)", lambda: two_tasks(highs(2)))]: try: sol, dt = solve(make()) per_host = load(sol["assignment"], {"t0": 10.0, "t1": 10.0}) GATE[label] = sol print(f"{label:<28} -> host loads {dict(sorted(per_host.items()))} GB, endReason {ends(sol)}, " f"{dt * 1000:.1f} ms") except Exception as e: GATE[label] = None print(f"{label:<28} -> FAILED {clean(e)}") print("
What the build refuses (each is caught here; the message is the binding's own):") for label, make in [("OptimalSolverSpec() default", lambda: two_tasks(spec("optimalSolverSpec", suppressLogs=True))), ("solverPackage=1 (Gurobi)", lambda: two_tasks(spec("optimalSolverSpec", solverPackage=1, suppressLogs=True))), ('policy="HARD" (a name)', lambda: two_tasks(local_search(2), policy="HARD")), ('solverPackage="HIGHS"', lambda: two_tasks({"optimalSolverSpec": {"solverPackage": "HIGHS"}}))]: try: solve(make()) print(f" {label:<28} -> accepted") except Exception as e: print(f" {label:<28} -> {clean(e, 60)}") try: spec("localSearchSolverSpec", timeLimitMs=500) except KeyError as e: print(f" spec(..., timeLimitMs=500) -> {e.args[0]}") def gate_ok(sol): # solved means OPTIMAL and, by recount, no host above its 15 GB return (sol is not None and ends(sol) == "OPTIMAL" and len(sol["assignment"]) == 2 and max(load(sol["assignment"], {"t0": 10.0, "t1": 10.0}).values()) <= 15.0) HIGHS_OK = gate_ok(GAT
articles.summary: Meta의 작업 배치 최적화 도구 Rebalancer를 C++ 코어와 Python 바인딩으로 활용하고, 지역 탐색과 HiGHS 혼합정수 솔버를 비교하는 튜토리얼이다. 작성자는 해당 테스트 환경의 24회 실행 중 14회에서 메모리 용량을 초과한 배치에도 해결 상태가 참으로 표시됐으며, 일부 잘못된 설정 키도 조용히 무시됐다고 보고했다. 핵심 실무 교훈은 솔버의 상태 표시만 신뢰하지 말고 반환된 배치의 자원 사용량과 제약 충족 여부를 직접 검증해야 한다는 것이다. 결과는 특정 빌드와 Apple M4 환경에서 나온 것으로, 다른 버전이나 실행 환경에 그대로 일반화하기는 어렵다.

articles.title: Flox Intelligence is building AI to keep wildlife away from trains, airports, and roads
articles.content: Flox's edge devices can identify animals and use species-specific sounds to drive them away from critical infrastructure.
articles.summary: Flox Intelligence가 철도·공항·도로 주변의 야생동물을 식별하고 접근을 막는 AI 시스템을 개발하고 있다. 엣지 장치가 동물을 구분한 뒤 종별로 다른 소리를 사용해 주요 인프라에서 멀어지도록 유도하는 방식이다. 현장 인식과 대응을 결합한 AI 적용 사례로 동물과 교통시설 간 충돌 위험을 줄이는 데 활용될 수 있지만, 제공된 자료에는 식별 정확도나 퇴치 효과의 검증 수치가 없다.

articles.title: Facebook is giving users more control over their algorithm
articles.content: Meta announced the launch of its new AI-powered feature, “Your Algorithm,” a feature it first launched on Instagram.
articles.summary: Meta가 Instagram에서 먼저 선보인 AI 기반 기능 ‘Your Algorithm’을 Facebook에도 출시한다고 발표했다. 사용자에게 자신의 추천 알고리즘에 대한 더 많은 통제권을 제공하는 것이 핵심이다. 이용자가 콘텐츠 추천에 관여할 수 있는 제품 변화이지만, 제공된 자료에는 조정 가능한 항목이나 추천 결과에 미치는 구체적인 영향이 설명돼 있지 않다.

articles.title: Pluto Security raises $42M as AI gives enterprise security teams a new headache
articles.content: The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon.
articles.summary: Pluto Security가 4,200만 달러를 조달했으며, 기사는 기업 내 AI 도구 확산으로 생기는 보안 우려를 배경으로 제시한다. 직원들이 AI를 예상하지 못한 방식으로 사용하면서 기존 시스템에 새로운 보안 공백이 생길 수 있다는 것이 핵심 문제의식이다. 기업 AI 도입과 함께 보안 관리 수요도 커지고 있음을 보여주지만, 제공된 자료에는 Pluto Security의 구체적인 방어 기술이나 검증된 성과가 없다.

articles.title: Judge orders OpenAI to turn over hiring records in Apple trade secrets case
articles.content: A federal judge ruled that Apple can access OpenAI's interview materials involving former Apple employees, as well as private messages and testimony from key figures in the case.
articles.summary: 미국 연방 판사가 Apple 영업비밀 사건에서 Apple이 전직 직원과 관련된 OpenAI의 면접 자료에 접근할 수 있도록 결정했다. 접근 대상에는 사건 주요 인물의 비공개 메시지와 증언도 포함된다. 모델 기술 발표가 아니라 AI 기업의 인재 채용과 영업비밀 관리에 관한 법적 사건이며, 이번 자료 접근 결정 자체가 위법 행위를 확정한 것은 아니다.

articles.title: SpaceXSI bundles X Premium, Grok, and Cursor into one subscription
articles.content: The new X Subscription combines X's paid features with AI tools like Grok and Cursor, offering plans ranging from $8 to $200 per month.
articles.summary: 보도에 따르면 새로운 X Subscription은 X의 유료 기능과 Grok·Cursor 같은 AI 도구를 하나의 구독 체계로 묶는다. 요금제 범위는 월 8~200달러로 제시됐다. 소셜 서비스와 AI 활용 도구를 결합한 상품 구성이라는 의미가 있지만, 제공된 자료에는 각 요금제에 포함되는 기능이나 사용 한도가 없어 개별 구독 대비 경제성을 판단하기 어렵다.

articles.title: Cerebras CEO says we’re nearing a future where everyone has a personal AI assistant at home
articles.content: Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman predicts a future where personal AI assistants become as commonplace as household appliances, running partly on local devices and partly in the cloud.
articles.summary: Cerebras의 Andrew Feldman CEO가 개인용 AI 비서가 가전제품처럼 보편화될 미래를 전망했다. 그는 이러한 비서가 일부 기능은 로컬 기기에서, 나머지는 클라우드에서 실행하는 형태가 될 것으로 내다봤다. 개인용 AI의 배치 방식에 대한 산업계 관점을 보여주지만, 이는 신제품 출시나 검증된 보급 전망이 아니라 경영진의 예측이다.

articles.title: Science Corporation implants its vision-restoring chip in its first Stargardt disease patient
articles.content: Max Hodak, the former president and co-founder of Neuralink, detailed on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt how his company's work with PRIMA is part of its path toward a novel brain-computer interface (BCI).
articles.summary: Science Corporation이 시력 회복용 칩을 첫 스타르가르트병 환자에게 이식했다는 보도다. Neuralink 공동창업자이자 전 사장인 Max Hodak은 TechCrunch Disrupt에서 PRIMA 관련 작업이 새로운 뇌-컴퓨터 인터페이스로 향하는 개발 경로의 일부라고 설명했다. 해당 질환 환자에 대한 이식 사례라는 의미가 있지만, 제공된 자료에는 시력 개선 정도나 장기 안전성 결과가 없어 치료 효과를 확정할 수 없다.
